clue.text: Substitute second one of three Shakespearean sisters

parts.note: s = second, the unit of time as abbreviated on a stopwatch
Macbeth opens with three of them stirring a cauldron, the weird sisters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Second one of three' sounds like an instruction to pick the middle sister out of the trio. It is nothing of the sort: the abbreviation comes first and the sister arrives whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Substitute → SWITCH: swapping one thing for another is switching it, so the two verbs trade places in a sentence without changing it.

clue.text: Obvious trail grew blurred

indicators.note: Something blurred has lost its clean edges, so the letters it is made of can no longer be trusted to stay where they were put.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a path fading into the distance, which is why 'blurred' reads as description rather than instruction. Nothing looks like fodder until you count those two words against the enumeration.
explanation.definitionFit: Obvious → WRIT LARGE: something writ large is set down in letters big enough for anyone to read, so it is obvious in the sense of unmissable.

clue.text: Children anxious when putting electronics together

indicators.note: Electronic things are the e- things, so the electronics here are the two Es of the fodder, and pushing that pair together drags every other letter out of place.

parts.note: an anxious person is tense, and those five letters are the fodder

explanation.walkthrough: Most anagram indicators just say 'these letters move'. This one names exactly which letters travel, and the surface — a family wrestling with a gadget — makes 'putting together' read as construction.
explanation.definitionFit: Children → TEENS: teenagers are still children, so the plural noun defines the answer by age band rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Huge museum valued old stuff, bagging millions

indicators.note: A bag closes round whatever you drop into it, so the word doing the bagging has to open up and swallow the other piece.

parts.note: the buildings and customs a country keeps because they are old and valued are its heritage; this word splits after three letters
m = million, as written on a salary or a budget

explanation.walkthrough: A museum valuing old stuff and taking in millions is exactly what museums do, so the second half of the clue reads as more description and never as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Huge museum → HERMITAGE: the Hermitage in St Petersburg is one of the largest museums on earth, so the definition names the answer by example.

clue.text: Outside in deluge, fellow gets drier in the car

indicators.note: The outside of a word is the letter at each end, and those two are all that is kept of the downpour.

parts.note: the first and last letters of DELUGE, the middle of the word washed away
a fellow is a mister, the everyday title for a man

explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside' looks like part of the rainy picture rather than an instruction, and that is the whole disguise. Every word of the surface is weather; the answer is the gadget that fights it.
explanation.definitionFit: drier in the car → DEMISTER: the demister blows warm air across the windscreen to dry the film of mist off it, so it really is the car's drier.

clue.text: 500 pies to supply store

indicators.note: Read it as the adverb from supple, not the verb everyone expects: done in a bending, flexible way, and letters that bend do not keep their order.

parts.note: D is 500 in Roman numerals
the six letters of PIES TO, bent into a new order

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a bakery order, and the misdirection is grammatical: the one word carrying the instruction looks like the plain verb it is pronounced nothing like.
explanation.definitionFit: store → DEPOSIT: to deposit something is to put it somewhere for safekeeping, the bank's sense of storing it rather than a shop.

clue.text: Our team runs after flash vehicle driven on the pitch?

indicators.note: 'After' sends the pieces it introduces to the back, so the pair named first in the clue ends up second in the answer.

parts.note: a flash is a moment, and a moment is a mo — 'back in a mo'
the team we belong to is 'we', first person plural
r = runs on a cricket scorecard, where a batter's runs are totted up

explanation.walkthrough: Read as English it is a chase — our lot running after a flash motor — and the answer is groundsman's kit. A pitch here is the playing surface, not a sales pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: vehicle driven on the pitch? → MOWER: a ride-on mower is the one machine allowed to drive on a sports pitch, and the question mark admits 'vehicle' is loose.

clue.text: Welfare services in Worcestershire going up, an alarming figure

indicators.note: Welfare that goes 'in' a county sits inside it rather than beside it, so the county's letters open up and close again around it.
This is a down entry, so a name going up is read from the bottom of the grid towards the top.

parts.note: Worcestershire is an English county and WORCS is its standard short form, seen on envelopes and road signs; here it climbs the grid
welfare services are care — social care, care in the community

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a news item about council funding, so not one word of it looks like an instruction. The county abbreviation is the piece a solver outside Britain has to be told.
explanation.definitionFit: an alarming figure → SCARECROW: it is a figure standing in a field whose entire job is to alarm birds, so both words of the definition are literal.

clue.text: What some pappardelle at Enzo's might be?

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part rather than the whole, and the part it wants is a run of letters already sitting in the words around it.

parts.note: five letters run consecutively through these words, straddling both gaps

explanation.walkthrough: Pappardelle is a broad ribbon pasta and Enzo's is any Italian restaurant you care to name. The clue is a plain question that also spells its own answer out.
explanation.definitionFit: Read the whole question as the definition: pasta ordered in an Italian restaurant is very likely to end up eaten, and the same words hide the letters.

clue.text: Dangerous building's engineers caught by appropriate criminal charge

indicators.note: Something caught by a word is held inside it rather than added on the end, so those letters land in the middle.

parts.note: appropriate = fit, as in 'fit for purpose'; it opens after two letters
RE = Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps and crosswords' standard engineers
a rap is a criminal charge — 'taking the rap', 'a murder rap'

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all inspectors and courtrooms, which is why 'appropriate' reads as an adjective describing the charge rather than as a word waiting to be prised open.
explanation.definitionFit: Dangerous building → FIRETRAP: a firetrap is a building with no safe way out of it if it burns, so the danger named is that specific one.

clue.text: Plenty breaking the law

indicators.note: Something broken comes apart into its pieces, and pieces swept back together rarely land in the order they started in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.walkthrough: Four words, and three of them are machinery: the whole clue reads as a headline about crime while the definition sits in the very first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Plenty → WEALTH: a wealth of something is an abundance of it, the mass-noun sense rather than money in a bank account.

clue.text: Doctor photos including bottom, prick and leg

indicators.note: What a word includes goes inside it, so the photos have to open up and take the other piece into themselves.

parts.note: photos are pics, and this word opens after its first letter
the bottom of a league table is last
to prick someone on is to urge or spur them into action
in cricket the leg side of the field is also the on side, so 'leg' regularly means ON

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' at the head of a clue nearly always means shuffle these letters, and here it is the definition. The crudest-looking words in the surface turn out to be the honest ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctor → PLASTIC SURGEON: 'doctor' is the broad word for any qualified medic and the answer is one specialism of it, a definition by class rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Rose planted in west-facing flower garden

indicators.note: Something planted in a bed is buried inside it untouched, which is what these letters are doing in the words that follow.
This is an across entry, so letters facing west are read from the right-hand end back towards the left.

parts.note: four letters in a row straddle the gap between these two words, and the entry travels back through them

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is gardening from end to end, so every word looks like scenery. The definition is the one word that also names a flower, which is precisely why it leads.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose → GREW: a plant that rose is one that grew, the past tense of the verb rather than the bloom the surface is waving at you.

clue.text: Spooner's low-alcohol champagne perhaps driver's limit

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner was famous for trading the opening sounds of two words, so his name alone is the instruction to swap them.

parts.note: a drink low in alcohol is a light one, and it hands its opening sound over to its neighbour
champagne is one example of wine, and it collects the sound the other word gave up

explanation.walkthrough: Say the plain version aloud first — a light wine is exactly what the surface is offering — and the swap does the rest. What comes out is painted on a road.
explanation.definitionFit: driver's limit → WHITE LINE: the white line down a road is the boundary a driver is not meant to cross, the same idea as 'crossing the line'.

clue.text: Gold fried tortilla filled by Romeo the Italian way

parts.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold

indicators.note: Whatever fills a thing is inside it, so the tortilla closes around the letter that follows.

parts.note: a tostada is a flat fried tortilla in Mexican cooking; it splits open after four letters
R is Romeo in the radio alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: Two of the three pieces are conventions rather than words, a chemical symbol and a radio-alphabet letter, and the surface's Mexican kitchen has nothing to do with the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: the Italian way → AUTOSTRADA: an autostrada is Italy's motorway, so 'way' is the road sense and 'Italian' says whose roads are meant.

clue.text: Boiling southern trip

parts.note: water boiling is seething, and so is a person in a temper
S = southern, as on a compass or a railway's name

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, and the join between them is invisible: the whole clue reads as a description of a bad-tempered journey to the south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: trip → SEE THINGS: to trip is to hallucinate, and someone hallucinating sees things that are not there — both are the informal drug sense.

clue.text: Flip deep-fried pastry, pinching runny nose

indicators.note: To pinch a thing is to take it, and what a word takes it keeps inside itself rather than alongside.
Something runny has lost its shape and will not hold a form, so its letters do not stay in the order they were given.

parts.note: a deep-fried ring of pastry is a donut, spelled the short American way; it opens after two letters
the four letters of NOSE, run together in a different order

explanation.walkthrough: A runny nose and a doughnut make one greasy picture, which is why neither word looks like an instruction until the enumeration refuses to fit.
explanation.definitionFit: Flip → DO ONE'S NUT: to flip, or flip your lid, is to lose your temper, and doing your nut is the British idiom for the same explosion.

clue.text: Slow and careful French composer reduced tempo

indicators.note: A reduced word has been cut short, and what a cut takes off a name is the letter standing at its end.

parts.note: Léo Delibes wrote Coppélia and Lakmé; cut short, his name loses its final S
the tempo of a thing is the rate it goes at

explanation.walkthrough: The definition wants the unhurried sense of the word rather than the 'done on purpose' one, and Delibes is the sort of nineteenth-century name crosswords keep in circulation.
explanation.definitionFit: Slow and careful → DELIBERATE: a deliberate movement is an unhurried, considered one, the adjective's taking-its-time sense rather than its intentional one.

clue.text: Sell uranium which military operation has seized

indicators.note: Something seized is grabbed and held on to, so the word doing the seizing closes around what it has taken.

parts.note: a military operation is an action — troops are said to see action
U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an arms-trade news item, which makes 'seized' read as confiscation by the authorities rather than as an instruction to swallow a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Sell → AUCTION: to auction goods is to sell them to the highest bidder, so the definition is the general verb and the answer one particular way of doing it.

clue.text: Strand unwound from ball left on court

indicators.note: In an across clue a piece sitting 'on' another follows it, the way a rider sits on a horse and is read second.

parts.note: to court someone is to woo them
L = left, as marked in stage directions and on a pair of boots

explanation.walkthrough: Tennis is the picture the surface wants — a ball, a court, a line call — and the answer is knitting. 'On' is doing positional work in a clue full of sporting prepositions.
explanation.definitionFit: Strand unwound from ball → WOOL: what you unwind from a ball of wool is a strand of wool, so the phrase names the answer by where it comes off.

clue.text: Doctor's cleverer friend treated more shell shock

indicators.note: A patient treated is worked on and comes out altered, and letters that have been worked on come out in a different arrangement.

parts.note: anagram fodder, fourteen letters

explanation.walkthrough: Shell shock and a doctor build a first-world-war surface with nothing to do with Baker Street, and that distance is what keeps a fourteen-letter anagram out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctor's cleverer friend → SHERLOCK HOLMES: Dr Watson is the doctor, and his flatmate is the one who always sees what Watson has missed.

clue.text: Hot-tub party being made sexless

parts.note: a hot tub is the centrepiece of a spa
a do is a party in everyday British usage — 'a bit of a do'

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is far kinder than the answer: a solver who has never met this word can still build it from two of the friendliest short words in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: being made sexless → SPADO: a spado is a eunuch, a castrated man — a rare Latin-derived word that survives mostly in dictionaries and grids.

clue.text: Sensible group of investigators has uncovered clue first

indicators.note: A word uncovered has had the letters at each end taken off it, its covering stripped from both sides at once.
'First' sends the piece it labels to the head of the answer, ahead of the letters clued before it.

parts.note: cLUe with the letters at both ends stripped away
the CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the detective branch of a British police force

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a police procedural, which is exactly why 'clue' reads as part of the plot rather than as four letters waiting to be trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Sensible → LUCID: a lucid person is clear-headed and talking sense, the in-one's-right-mind sense of sensible rather than the practical one.

clue.text: Anaesthetic that's laughter-inducing, about to be inhaled

indicators.note: Whatever is inhaled ends up inside the thing breathing it in, so this piece goes into the middle of the other.

parts.note: LOL is what you type for laughing out loud; it splits open after two letters
ca. is short for circa, Latin for about, used before an approximate date

explanation.walkthrough: Laughing gas is the surface's joke — nitrous oxide really is an inhaled anaesthetic that leaves patients giggling — and the definition sits in the very first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Anaesthetic → LOCAL: doctors shorten 'local anaesthetic' to 'a local', so the adjective stands in for the whole phrase.

clue.text: Mother with 50p, say, brought back root vegetable

indicators.note: This is an across entry, so a piece brought back is read from right to left and arrives with its letters in reverse.

parts.note: ma = mother, the nursery word
a 50p piece, the British fifty-pence, is one example of a coin — and here it is turned round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is the setter flagging an example rather than a synonym: the value is irrelevant, all that matters is that it names a coin.
explanation.definitionFit: root vegetable → MANIOC: manioc is cassava, the starchy tropical root that tapioca is made from, so it is a root vegetable in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Old pope inside rather than outside church, and disrobed

indicators.note: What is outside goes round what is inside, so the piece named here wraps itself about the letters that follow.
Robes come off the outside, so a disrobed word loses its first and last letters and keeps what was covered up.

parts.note: inside is simply in — the word itself, not an abbreviation
'walk rather than drive' is 'walk and not drive', so the phrase hands over not; this word splits open after two letters
CE = Church of England, the church in a crossword unless another is named
the word 'and' with its outer letters taken off leaves N

explanation.walkthrough: Read as English it is a scene: a pope indoors rather than out at church, and stripped of his robes. Every one of those words is an instruction instead. 'Rather than' is the hardest — it is standing in for NOT — and 'and' is a word to be worked on here, not a joiner.
explanation.definitionFit: Old pope → INNOCENT: thirteen popes took the name Innocent, the last of them in 1721, so the definition names the answer by example.

clue.text: Attitude I assume is Olympian

parts.note: a pose is an attitude struck for effect
the setter's own I, taken simply as the letter
to don a coat is to assume it — to put it on

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a boast about one's own bearing, and the joke is that the Olympian turns out to be a god of the sea rather than a lofty manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Olympian → POSEIDON: he is one of the twelve gods of Olympus, so the definition names the family the answer belongs to rather than a synonym.

clue.text: US et al organised simultaneous gunfire, say

indicators.note: Organising a group means arranging it into a new order, which is what happens to the six letters standing in front of the word.

parts.note: anagram fodder, six letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'US et al' looks like a list of allies in a news report, and the enumeration is the only hint that it is six letters waiting to be shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: simultaneous gunfire, say → SALUTE: a gun salute is one kind of salute, and 'say' warns that the definition is naming an example rather than the whole word.
